title: Indian IT Shift: Routine Jobs Face AI Pressure, Specialist Skills in Demand
excerpt: Large-scale layoffs are behind Indian IT, recruiters say, but targeted exits and selective backfilling are reshaping hiring — with AI fluency now the decisive dividing line.
body:
• India's IT jobs market is undergoing a structural shift: companies are cutting mid-career and routine roles while selectively hiring specialist freshers and AI experts, with FY27 hiring expected to stay subdued.
  • The roles under the greatest pressure are repetitive, rules-based work — entry-level coding, routine testing, basic application maintenance and data processing — plus coordination-heavy middle-management layers being redesigned as AI augments or automates them.
  • Hiring demand is concentrating around AI/ML, cloud, data science, cybersecurity and automation, while junior and mid-level engineers without AI fluency face the highest displacement risk.
  • Despite restructuring, overall industry employment grew about 1.35 lakh in FY26; revenue is rising while headcount grows more slowly, signalling a move from headcount-led to productivity-led growth.

What is actually happening inside Indian IT in 2026 is more structural than the headlines suggest. Large-scale layoffs appear to be behind the industry, but targeted exits, thinner middle layers and selective backfilling are quietly reordering who gets hired and who does not.

The headline numbers mask a split. The top five IT services companies — TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro and Tech Mahindra — reduced their combined headcount by nearly 7,000 in FY26, with TCS alone cutting more than 23,000 while Infosys added around 5,000. Yet at the industry level, employment still grew by about 1.35 lakh in FY26, marginally above the 1.33 lakh added in FY25. "Revenue is growing, but headcount is growing at a slightly slower pace," Neeti Sharma, CEO of TeamLease Digital, told The Times of India. "The industry is becoming more selective about which skills it hires and which roles it continues to invest in."

Employees leaving are increasingly not being replaced one-for-one. Companies are leaving positions vacant, redistributing work and hiring for a different skill set altogether — a calibrated approach that analysts describe as workforce transformation rather than contraction.

Context & Background

The shift follows the post-pandemic correction. In 2022 and 2023, technology companies shed excess capacity built during the hiring boom through high-volume layoffs. Having done that downsizing, large firms have kept headcounts controlled through two-plus years of lowered hiring, according to Anil Ethanur, co-founder of staffing firm Xpheno.

What is different in 2026 is the driver: artificial intelligence. "If 2025 was about correcting over-hiring during the pandemic, 2026 is increasingly about redesigning organisations for the AI era," TeamLease's research notes. Companies are targeting duplicated roles and bloated management structures — quietly, through performance-linked exits and skill-based restructuring rather than press releases. An estimated 35,000 "silent" job cuts are expected across Indian tech in 2026 as firms accelerate AI adoption, according to industry trackers.

Impact & Analysis

The roles facing the greatest pressure are those built around repetitive, rules-based, highly standardised work — particularly where AI can automate or significantly augment existing processes. "This includes some entry-level coding, routine testing, basic application maintenance and repetitive data-processing activities," Milind Shah, managing director of Randstad Digital India, told TOI. "However, this is not simply a story of technology jobs disappearing; it is a story of the skills required within those jobs changing."

Junior and mid-level engineers are the most exposed, Ethanur says, since low-complexity roles and engineering output were traditionally assigned to them. But the pressure extends upward: enterprise AI platforms can reach across low, mid and high cognitive layers, and the pace of AI development could challenge experienced specialists too in the coming years.

"Enterprise grade AI has a potential to impact 40% to 60% of the tech workforce that's engaged in low and mid cognitive functions."

— Anil Ethanur, Co-founder, Xpheno

On the other side, hiring is concentrating around AI/ML, cloud, data science, cybersecurity and automation. "Professionals with AI fluency alongside expertise in areas such as cloud, data, cybersecurity, automation and digital engineering will increasingly be in demand," Shah said. "The ability to combine technical knowledge with problem-solving, domain expertise and client-facing skills will become particularly important."

"The bigger risk is not necessarily that a particular role disappears, but that the old version of that job becomes less relevant."

— Neeti Sharma, CEO, TeamLease Digital

Attrition data reinforces the two-track market. Voluntary attrition at large IT services firms has normalised to 13-14%, but people with AI, cloud and cybersecurity skills retain mobility while routine roles face restructuring. Randstad found nearly one in four technology professionals globally have left a job over inadequate upskilling — attrition driven as much by employees chasing future-ready skills as by restructuring.

Diaspora Angle

The same restructuring is visible in every market where Indian engineers work. For NRI tech professionals — particularly in the US, where AI-driven layoffs have coincided with tighter H-1B scrutiny — the Indian data offers a leading indicator: the roles under pressure are the same ones (routine coding, testing, support), and the insurance is the same (AI fluency paired with domain expertise).

What's Next

The consensus is that FY27 hiring will remain subdued, with attrition backfilled selectively and Performance Improvement Plans replacing blanket layoffs as the main exit mechanism. Randstad's Workmonitor study found 95% of employers globally expect their organisations to grow in 2026 — but growth and headcount growth are decoupling. For IT professionals, the question is no longer whether jobs are available, but which version of the job survives.
